subject: industrial-systems
audience: FE Industrial & Systems candidates and industrial engineering students
title: The 5% Defect Lot That Was Accepted 73.6% of the Time, Not 95%
featured_title: THE 5 PERCENT DEFECT LOT ACCEPTED 73.6 PERCENT OF THE TIME NOT 95

presentation.challenge: A 5% defective process did not imply a 95% lot-acceptance probability. Under an n=20, c=1 plan, acceptance required observing zero or one defective item.

practice.primary_question: How is lot acceptance probability calculated for a single-sampling plan using the binomial model?
practice.typical_exam_trap: Treating 1-p, the probability that one item is good, as the probability that an entire lot passes a multi-item sampling plan.

case_dna.target_misconception: If a lot is 5% defective, its probability of acceptance must be 95%.
case_dna.why_plausible: Ninety-five percent is the probability that one randomly selected item is nondefective, but a sampling plan evaluates the number of defectives in an entire sample.
case_dna.corrected_model: For a binomial single-sampling plan with sample size n and acceptance number c, calculate P(accept)=Σ from x=0 to c of C(n,x)p^x(1-p)^(n-x).

problem_statement: A single-sampling inspection plan selects n=20 items from a large lot and accepts the lot if at most c=1 defective item is found. Assume independent items and a true defective fraction p=0.05. A note states that the lot will be accepted 95% of the time because 95% of items are good. Determine the actual lot-acceptance probability using the binomial model.

gates.label: Incident
gates.heading: Item quality was mistaken for lot acceptance probability.
gates.prompt: Which sample outcomes lead to acceptance?

options.label: Use P(X≤1)=P(X=0)+P(X=1)
options.reason: The sampling plan accepts exactly those two binomial outcomes.

options.label: Use 1-p=0.95
options.reason: That is the probability one item is good, not the probability the 20-item sample contains at most one defective.

options.label: Use only P(X=1)
options.reason: A sample with zero defectives is also accepted.

gates.label: Predict
gates.heading: Predict the lot-acceptance probability
gates.prompt: Enter acceptance probability as a percentage.

gates.label: Experiment
gates.heading: Evaluate the sampling plan
gates.result: The lot is accepted with probability about 73.6%.

gates.label: Gap
gates.heading: Prove the acceptance probability
gates.hint: The two accepted outcomes are X=0 and X=1.

gates.label: Evidence
gates.heading: A sampling plan evaluates a distribution of possible sample counts

gates.label: Redline
gates.heading: Correct the sampling-plan note
report: C2. Each individual item is good with probability 95%.
C3. Therefore the n=20, c=1 plan accepts the lot with probability 95%.

claims.label: C1
claims.reason: This is the stated process defective fraction.

claims.label: C2
claims.reason: For one item, the nondefective probability is indeed 0.95.

claims.label: C3
claims.reason: Lot acceptance depends on the binomial count of defectives across all 20 sampled items.

evidence_choices.label: P(X≤1)=0.73584
evidence_choices.reason: This sums all sample outcomes allowed by the acceptance rule.

gates.label: Design Fix
gates.heading: Evaluate the same plan at 2% defective

options.label: Acceptance probability is exactly 98%
options.reason: 98% is the probability one item is good, not the sample-plan acceptance probability.

options.label: Acceptance probability stays 73.6%
options.reason: Changing p changes the binomial distribution.

gates.label: Transfer
gates.heading: Tighten the acceptance number
gates.prompt: For p=0.05 and n=20, what is the acceptance probability if c=0?

options.label: About 35.85%
options.reason: Only zero defectives are accepted, so P=0.95^20≈0.35849.
That is the result for c=1.
That again confuses single-item quality with lot acceptance.

gates.explanation: A stricter acceptance number lowers the probability of accepting a lot at the same defect level.

gates.label: Sign Off
gates.heading: Sign off the acceptance-sampling calculation
gates.confirmation: I confirm that lot acceptance probability comes from the distribution of defect counts in the sample, not directly from the fraction of good individual items.

items.label: What failed
items.value: Single-item conformance probability was reported as lot acceptance probability.

items.label: What was missed
items.value: The sampling plan accepts only particular binomial sample-count outcomes.

items.label: Corrected model
items.value: Sum binomial probabilities from zero defectives through the acceptance number c.

seo.meta_description: Solve FE Industrial & Systems Case E-090: for n=20, c=1, and p=0.05, the lot acceptance probability is 73.58%, not 95%.
seo.focus_keyphrase: FE Industrial acceptance sampling binomial probability
seo.excerpt: The fraction of good items is not the same as the probability that a lot passes a multi-item sampling plan.

faqs.q: How is acceptance probability calculated for a single-sampling plan?
faqs.a: Sum the binomial probabilities from zero defectives through the acceptance number c.

faqs.q: What happens if the acceptance number is reduced from 1 to 0?
faqs.a: Acceptance probability decreases because only samples with zero defectives pass.
